claim: Rho-family GTPases regulate cell polarity.
source: The diversity of cell morphologies arises, in part, through regulation of cell polarity by Rho-family GTPases.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citation to established literature in the introduction.

claim: Mass-conserved activator-substrate (MCAS) models develop multiple initial polarity sites that engage in competition, leaving a single winner.
source: Mass-conserved activator-substrate (MCAS) models that describe polarity circuits develop multiple initial polarity sites, but then those sites engage in competition, leaving a single winner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by theoretical analyses cited in the introduction.

claim: Competition slows dramatically as GTPase concentrations at polarity sites approach a saturation point.
source: Theoretical analyses predicted that competition would slow dramatically as GTPase concentrations at different polarity sites increase toward a 'saturation point', allowing polarity sites to coexist.
evidence: This prediction is stated in the abstract and is based on theoretical analyses referenced in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing the amount of key polarity proteins in budding yeast results in multiple polarity sites and simultaneous budding.
source: Here, we test this prediction using budding yeast cells, and confirm that increasing the amount of key polarity proteins results in multiple polarity sites and simultaneous budding.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Cells can switch from competition to equalization among polarity sites through a novel design principle.
source: Further, we elucidate a novel design principle whereby cells can switch from competition to equalization among polarity sites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results presented in Figure 5.

claim: Eukaryotic cells display a wide diversity of cell morphologies that are critical for specialized cell functions.
source: Eukaryotic cells display a very wide diversity of cell morphologies, which are often critical to carry out specialized cell functions.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Different morphologies arise through specific arrangements and actions of the cytoskeleton.
source: Different morphologies arise through specific arrangements and actions of the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The cytoskeleton is regulated by the conserved Rho family of GTPases.
source: In turn, the cytoskeleton is regulated by the conserved Rho family of GTPases (Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Rho-family GTPases (Cdc42, Rac, Rop) regulate cell polarity by concentrating at regions of the plasma membrane.
source: A subset of these GTPases (Cdc42, Rac, Rop) regulates cell polarity by concentrating at one or more regions of the plasma membrane (Park and Bi, 2007; Wu and Lew, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In many cell types, it is crucial to maintain one and only one polarity domain.
source: In many cell types (e.g. migrating cells, plant pollen tubes, and root hairs or diverse budding yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans, and Ustilago maydis), it is crucial to maintain one and only one polarity domain, establishing a single polarity axis (front) that leads to movement or growth in that direction (Chiou et al., 2017; Houk et al., 2012; Wu and Lew, 2013; Yang and Lavagi, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with specific examples and supported by citations.

claim: In other cell types, multiple active-GTPase polarity sites coexist in the same cell.
source: In other cell types (e.g. neurons with many neurite tips, plant cells that form xylem, or filamentous fungal cells with branches), multiple active-GTPase polarity sites coexist in the same cell (Dotti et al., 1988; Knechtle et al., 2003; Oda and Fukuda, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with specific examples and supported by citations.

claim: Interacting biochemical networks with positive feedback and differential diffusion can generate spontaneous pattern formation.
source: It has long been appreciated that interacting biochemical networks that include positive feedback and differential diffusion of reactants can generate systems capable of spontaneous pattern formation (Meinhardt, 2008; Meinhardt and Gierer, 1974; Turing, 1952).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: MCAS models consist of sets of partial differential equations encoding interconversion between membrane-bound activator and cytosolic substrate.
source: These models consist of sets of partial differential equations (PDEs) that encode the interconversion of polarity factors between two forms: a membrane-bound (and hence slow-diffusing) 'activator' and a cytosolic (and hence rapidly diffusing) 'substrate' (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MCAS models feature positive feedback where membrane regions with higher activator concentrations recruit more substrate from the cytoplasm.
source: One critical feature of these systems is positive feedback, such that membrane regions with higher concentrations of activator can locally recruit and activate more substrate from the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a critical feature of MCAS models.

claim: MCAS models feature differential diffusivity between activator and substrate.
source: A second critical feature is the difference in diffusivity between the activator and the substrate, allowing a localized accumulation of activator to recruit substrate from a much wider region of cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a critical feature of MCAS models.

claim: MCAS models feature mass conservation where the combined amount of activator and substrate is fixed.
source: A third critical feature is mass conservation: because the combined amount of activator and substrate is fixed, accumulation of activator at the membrane depletes substrate from the cytoplasm, limiting the size, activator concentration, and potentially the number of permissible activator-enriched regions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a critical feature of MCAS models.

claim: In the minimalistic MCAS model, peak activator concentration approaches a saturation point as total protein amount increases.
source: In the minimalistic model, as total protein amount in the system increases, peak u concentration (red) approaches a saturation point while basal v concentration (blue) declines to a limit.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1D legend and shown in the figure.

claim: In the minimalistic MCAS model, basal substrate concentration declines to a limit as total protein amount increases.
source: In the minimalistic model, as total protein amount in the system increases, peak u concentration (red) approaches a saturation point while basal v concentration (blue) declines to a limit.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1D legend and shown in the figure.

claim: With peaks far from saturation, the larger peak depletes more substrate than the smaller peak, leading to competition.
source: With peaks far from saturation, the larger peak depletes more substrate than the smaller (Left panel, starting protein amounts 0.6x, 1x), leading to a net flux of substrate (arrow) that results in competition.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1E legend and illustrated in the figure.

claim: With peaks close to saturation, substrate depletion is similar for both peaks, leading to coexistence.
source: With peaks close to saturation, substrate depletion is similar for both (Right panel, starting protein amounts 2x, 4x), leading to little flux and therefore coexistence.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1E legend and illustrated in the figure.

claim: In the mechanistic model of yeast polarity, GTP-Cdc42 recruits its own GEF through interactions with PAKs and Bem1, yielding positive feedback.
source: GTP-Cdc42 binds effector p21-activated kinases (PAKs)(Bose et al., 2001; Cvrcková et al., 1995; Lamson et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 1995), which bind the scaffold protein Bem1 (Bose et al., 2001; Leeuw et al., 1995), which binds the GEF Cdc24 that activates Cdc42 (Bose et al., 2001; Butty et al., 2002; Ito et al., 2001; Peterson et al., 1994; Rapali et al., 2017). These interactions allow GTP-Cdc42 to recruit its own GEF, activating neighboring Cdc42 to yield positive feedback (Johnson et al., 2011; Kozubowski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Competition time increases as peaks saturate in the mechanistic model.
source: Competition time increases as peaks saturate.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1I legend and shown in the figure.

claim: The mechanistic model exhibits saturation similar to minimalistic models.
source: We first asked whether a multi-species mechanistic 2D model of the budding yeast system (Goryachev and Pokhilko, 2008; Wu et al., 2015) behaved in a similar manner to the minimalistic models in terms of saturation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by simulation data in Figure 1G-H.

claim: In the mechanistic model, cytoplasmic substrate Bem1-GEF is depleted and reaches a plateau when total amounts of Cdc42 and Bem1-GEF are increased in parallel.
source: When the total amounts of both Cdc42 and Bem1-GEF were increased in parallel, the cytoplasmic substrate Bem1-GEF was depleted and quickly reached a plateau (Figure 1G,H), similar to substrate depletion in the minimalistic model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: In the mechanistic model, levels of cytoplasmic substrate Cdc42 increase when total amounts of Cdc42 and Bem1-GEF are increased in parallel.
source: In contrast, levels of the cytoplasmic substrate Cdc42 increased, indicating that this substrate was in excess and failed to saturate (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In a multi-component system, saturation is only seen for the limiting species.
source: We conclude that similar to minimalistic models, the mechanistic model exhibits saturation. However, in a multi-component system saturation is only seen for the limiting species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Saturation leads to coexistence in the mechanistic model.
source: We next asked whether saturation leads to coexistence in the mechanistic model. When simulations were initiated with two unequal peaks, competition occurred rapidly with low protein amounts, but slowed in a non-linear manner as the total amount of protein in the system was increased (Figure 1I), generating competition times that would be long compared to the yeast bud emergence timescale.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Cells should switch from competition to coexistence as the amount of polarity activators in peaks increases.
source: A simple prediction emerging from the polarity models discussed above is that cells should switch from competition to coexistence as the amount of polarity 'activators' in the peaks increase.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the Results section based on the modeling results.

claim: Extreme overexpression or global optogenetic activation of polarity proteins leads primarily to depolarization.
source: Indeed, previous work indicated that extreme overexpression or global optogenetic activation of polarity proteins leads primarily to depolarization, with only occasional multi-polarity (Howell et al., 2012; Howell et al., 2009; Lamas et al., 2020; Silva et al., 2019; Witte et al., 2017; Ziman and Johnson, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increasing cell size while keeping protein concentrations constant should lead to multi-budded cells.
source: A more robust way to generate multiple polarity domains would be to increase the size of cell while keeping overall protein concentrations constant (Chiou et al., 2018; Ishihara et al., 2007): this should lead to multi-budded cells while avoiding depolarized outcomes.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The cdc12-6 mutant is defective in cytokinesis at 37°C, generating chains of elongated, connected cells.
source: The temperature-sensitive septin mutant cdc12-6 is defective in cytokinesis at 37°C, generating chains of elongated, connected cells (Figure 2A, Video 1; Hartwell, 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section, shown in Figure 2A and Video 1, and supported by a citation.

claim: The cytoplasm is continuous between connected cells in cdc12-6 mutants.
source: Control experiments confirmed the continuity of the cytoplasm between the connected cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and showed that the concentration of polarity proteins remained constant as the cells grew larger (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the first cell cycle after switching to 37°C, all cdc12-6 cells generated a single bud.
source: In the first cell cycle after switching to 37°C, all cells generated a single bud, which remained connected to the mother.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the second cell cycle, most cdc12-6 cells formed a single bud despite having two cell bodies and two nuclei.
source: In the second cell cycle, most cells formed a single bud despite having two cell bodies and two nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A few cdc12-6 cells generated two buds simultaneously in the second cell cycle.
source: However, a few cells generated two buds simultaneously.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fraction of multi-budded cdc12-6 cells increased dramatically in the third and fourth cell cycles.
source: The fraction of multi-budded cells increased dramatically in the third and the fourth cell cycles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Similar multi-budded outcomes were observed in a conditional cytokinesis-defective iqg1 strain.
source: Similar multi-budded outcomes were observed in a conditional cytokinesis-defective iqg1 strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Shannon and Li, 1999), indicating that the phenotype is not specific to septin mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and supported by a citation.

claim: Larger cells with more polarity proteins can trigger a transition from competition to coexistence.
source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that larger cells with more polarity proteins (due to their larger volume) can trigger a transition from competition to coexistence.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental data.

claim: Diploid cdc12-6 cells have larger volume than haploid cdc12-6 cells.
source: Diploid cells have larger volume (and hence more polarity proteins) but also wider necks (which would provide a smaller impediment to diffusion) compared to haploids (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Diploid cdc12-6 cells have wider necks than haploid cdc12-6 cells.
source: Diploid cells have larger volume (and hence more polarity proteins) but also wider necks (which would provide a smaller impediment to diffusion) compared to haploids (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Larger diploid cdc12-6 cells generated significantly more two-budded cells than haploid cdc12-6 cells despite having wider necks.
source: Despite having wider necks, the larger diploids generated significantly more two-budded cells than did the haploids (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Multi-budded outcomes in cytokinesis-defective cells can be predominantly attributed to larger cell size.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that the large cells generated following failure of cytokinesis can yield multi-budded outcomes, and that such outcomes can be predominantly attributed to the larger cell size.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental data comparing haploid and diploid cells.

claim: Larger cell size could lead to multi-polar outcomes by affecting the number of initial polarity sites or subsequent competition between sites.
source: Larger cell size could lead to a multi-polar outcomes by affecting the number of polarity sites that initially form during polarity establishment, or the subsequent competition between sites, or both.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: Competition occurs both within individual cell compartments and between cell compartments connected by necks in cdc12-6 rsr1Δ cells.
source: Competition was evident both within individual cell compartments and between cell compartments connected by necks.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 3.

claim: Unipolar versus multipolar outcomes depend on both the number of initial polarity sites and whether they are eliminated by competition.
source: Thus, unipolar versus multipolar outcomes depend both on the number of initial polarity sites that form and on whether they are subsequently eliminated by competition.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The number of initial sites formed by cdc12-6 rsr1Δ cells increased in a manner correlated with cell length.
source: The number of initial sites formed by each cell increased in a manner correlated with cell length (Figure 4B), suggesting that cell length can influence initial polarization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Initial polarity sites in cdc12-6 rsr1Δ cells formed at non-random positions with a preference for bud tips and mother cell locations.
source: However, the locations at which initial sites formed were non-random, with a preference for bud tips and mother cell locations (Figure 4C), suggesting that (even without Rsr1) polarity may not initiate purely from molecular noise, and that geometric factors may bias the process.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When cdc12-6 rsr1Δ cells formed two initial sites, the distance between the sites was highly variable.
source: When cells formed two initial sites, the distance between the sites was highly variable (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The variable distance between initial polarity sites is consistent with MCAS models that have no preferred inter-peak length scale.
source: However, it is consistent with predictions from MCAS models that have no preferred inter-peak length scale (Goryachev and Leda, 2020; Goryachev and Pokhilko, 2008; Halatek et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The probability of successful competition between polarity sites decreased as cdc12-6 rsr1Δ cells grew larger.
source: Overall, the probability of successful competition between polarity sites decreased as cells grew larger, consistent with a transition from competition to coexistence regimes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Doubling the gene copy number of CDC42, CDC24, and BEM1 led to the expected increase in protein concentration.
source: Doubling the gene copy number led to the expected increase in the concentration of the encoded proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An extra copy of any single polarity gene did not greatly affect the frequency of multi-budded cells produced by cdc12-6 rsr1Δ mutants.
source: An extra copy of any single gene did not greatly affect the frequency of multi-budded cells produced by cdc12-6 rsr1Δ mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), consistent with previous overexpression reports in other strain backgrounds (Freisinger et al., 2013; Howell et al., 2012; Howell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and supported by citations.

claim: Doubling the gene copy number of CDC42, CDC24, and BEM1 did not affect cell morphology, volume, or length.
source: This did not affect the morphology, volume, or length of the cells (Figure 4F), and there was no systematic effect on the number of initial polarity sites formed (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Among cdc12-6 rsr1Δ cells that established two initial sites, the frequency of multi-polar outcomes was significantly increased when CDC42, CDC24, and BEM1 gene copy numbers were doubled.
source: However, among the cells that established two initial sites, the frequency of multi-polar outcomes was significantly increased (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Increasing the abundance of polarity proteins is sufficient to decrease the effectiveness of competition, yielding multi-polar outcomes.
source: We conclude that increasing the abundance of polarity proteins is sufficient to decrease the effectiveness of competition, yielding multi-polar outcomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Addition of a negative feedback loop to a minimalistic MCAS model did not enable equalization.
source: Addition of a negative feedback loop to a minimalistic model (Figure 5Ai) did not enable equalization (Chiou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Addition of negative feedback via activation of a Cdc42 GAP enabled equalization in a model.
source: However, addition of a negative feedback via activation of a Cdc42 GAP (Figure 5Aii; Jacobs et al., 2019) did enable equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Addition of negative feedback via inhibition of the GEF enabled equalization in the mechanistic model.
source: Addition of a negative feedback to our mechanistic model (Figure 1F) via inhibition of the GEF (simplified in Figure 5Aiii. Complete scheme in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) also enabled equalization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cdc42 promotes inhibitory phosphorylation of its GEF in yeast.
source: This mechanism was suggested by more recent experimental findings that Cdc42 promotes inhibitory phosphorylation of its GEF in yeast (Kuo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The key to equalization is the presence of an indirect pathway to convert activator into substrate.
source: Interestingly, the key to equalization in the hypothesis proposed above is not negative feedback per se, but rather the existence of a new species created by an activator that can generate a substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on analysis of different models.

claim: The indirect substrate model recapitulated the switch from competition to equalization behavior as total protein amount increased.
source: The new indirect substrate model recapitulated the switch from competition to equalization behavior as the total protein amount in the system was increased.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the indirect substrate model, basal levels of indirect substrate rose steadily as total protein amount increased.
source: Previously, at the single peak steady states of the minimalistic model (Figure 1D), basal levels of the cytoplasmic substrate v decreased until they reached a limit as the total protein amount in the system was increased. However, in the indirect substrate model, basal levels of vi rose steadily as the total protein amount was increased (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the indirect substrate model, basal level of substrate v initially decreased but then rose as total protein amount increased.
source: The basal level of substrate v initially decreased, but then rose as total protein amount was increased (Figure 5E), presumably due to flux from vi.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: When the larger peak was associated with lower substrate levels, the indirect substrate model displayed competition.
source: A key factor appeared to be the relative basal levels of cytoplasmic substrate associated with each peak: when the larger peak was associated with lower substrate levels, the system displayed competition; when the smaller peak was associated with lower substrate levels, the system displayed equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on simulation results shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: When the smaller peak was associated with lower substrate levels, the indirect substrate model displayed equalization.
source: A key factor appeared to be the relative basal levels of cytoplasmic substrate associated with each peak: when the larger peak was associated with lower substrate levels, the system displayed competition; when the smaller peak was associated with lower substrate levels, the system displayed equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on simulation results shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: The mobility of the indirect substrate must surpass a threshold in order to yield equalization.
source: This analysis confirmed that the mobility of the indirect substrate must surpass a threshold in order to yield equalization, and showed that equalization became the favored outcome as that mobility increased (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The difference between basal substrate levels associated with each peak precisely predicted the outcome of simulations.
source: In addition, the analysis confirmed that the difference between the basal substrate level associated with each peak precisely predicted the outcome of the simulations (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: When basal substrate was higher at the smaller peak, there was a flux of substrate toward the larger peak and the system displayed competition.
source: When basal substrate was higher at the smaller peak, there was a flux of substrate toward the larger peak and the system displayed competition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: When basal substrate was higher at the larger peak, there was a flux of substrate toward the smaller peak and the system displayed equalization.
source: When basal substrate was higher at the larger peak, there was a flux of substrate toward the smaller peak and the system displayed equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: When basal substrate was very similar at the two peaks, the system displayed coexistence.
source: When basal substrate was very similar at the two peaks, the system displayed coexistence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis shown in Figure 5I.

claim: All MCAS models can yield competition, but only models with indirect pathways to convert activator to substrate can yield equalization.
source: All MCAS models can yield competition, but only models with indirect pathways to convert activator to substrate can yield equalization, and this occurs regardless of whether the models have negative feedback.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on analysis of multiple models.

claim: Equalization occurs when local production of a mobile indirect substrate by the larger peak drives a flux of substrate toward the smaller peak.
source: Thus, equalization occurs when local production of a mobile indirect substrate by the larger peak drives a flux of substrate toward the smaller peak.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on analysis of the indirect substrate model.

claim: A non-phosphorylatable version of Cdc24 (Cdc2438A) did not diminish multipolar outcomes.
source: We constructed a mutant strain in which the wild-type Cdc24 (GEF) was replaced with a non-phosphorylatable version, Cdc2438A. This did not diminish multipolar outcomes: in fact, this strain made two-budded cells at a higher frequency than size-matched Cdc24-wild-type controls (of the second-cycle cells that established two initial sites, 65% of the Cdc2438A cells were two-budded compared to 12% of the Cdc24 cells).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental data.

claim: During equalization, two initially unequal peaks evolve toward two equal peaks.
source: During equalization, two initially unequal peaks evolve toward two equal peaks.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition of equalization.

claim: During coexistence, unequal peaks remain unequal.
source: During coexistence, unequal peaks remain unequal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a definition of coexistence.

claim: Negative feedback through Cdc24 phosphorylation can cause oscillation in the protein amount at each polarity peak.
source: A difficulty in distinguishing equalization and competition behaviors in cells with wild-type Cdc24 is that negative feedback through Cdc24 phosphorylation can cause oscillation in the protein amount at each polarity peak, obscuring the underlying processes (Howell et al., 2012; Kuo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The CDC2438A strain does not show oscillations in polarity peak protein amounts.
source: The CDC2438A strain short-circuits this negative feedback and does not show oscillations, allowing us to circumvent this complexity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the properties of the mutant.

claim: Among CDC2438A cells with two starting polarity sites, 15 cells exhibited competition.
source: These cells exhibited a continuum of behaviors that could almost all be classified as competition (15 cells: the larger peak grew and the smaller one shrank, Figure 6A) or coexistence (14 cells: the relative Bem1 amount in each peak stayed approximately constant, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Among CDC2438A cells with two starting polarity sites, 14 cells exhibited coexistence.
source: These cells exhibited a continuum of behaviors that could almost all be classified as competition (15 cells: the larger peak grew and the smaller one shrank, Figure 6A) or coexistence (14 cells: the relative Bem1 amount in each peak stayed approximately constant, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Three CDC2438A cells showed possible equalization where the larger peak shrank and the smaller one grew.
source: There were three cells in which quantification indicated that the larger peak shrank and the smaller one grew, consistent with equalization (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Instances of possible equalization were rare and their interpretation is uncertain.
source: However, these instances of possible equalization were rare, and their interpretation is dependent on quantification of a single timepoint (the last timepoint before budding), which leaves us uncertain as to whether they represent equalization or coexistence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a caveat about the equalization observations.

claim: Five CDC2438A cells with the slowest competition did not complete competition by the time of bud emergence and went on to grow two buds.
source: Interestingly, five of the cells with the slowest competition did not complete competition by the time of bud emergence, and went on to grow two buds (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Aborted competition appears to reflect slow competition curtailed by budding.
source: This phenotype, which we call 'aborted competition', appears to reflect slow competition curtailed by budding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the observed phenotype.

claim: Coexistence is the dominant mechanism for multipolar outcomes in yeast.
source: In aggregate, these data suggest that coexistence is the dominant reason for multipolar outcomes in yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Yeast cells behave as predicted by MCAS models, producing multipolar outcomes as the amount of polarity proteins increases.
source: Our findings expand on this work in three ways. First, we show experimentally that yeast cells behave as predicted by the models, producing multipolar outcomes as the amount of polarity proteins increases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: The key to equalization is the existence of additional species that provide indirect pathways to convert an activator into a substrate.
source: Second, we provide an explanation for a phenomenon called equalization, seen in more complex MCAS models, which can also produce multipolar outcomes. And third, we documented the dynamics of polarity sites in yeast cells, supporting coexistence as the dominant mechanism for multi-polar outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Coexistence is the dominant mechanism for multi-polar outcomes in yeast cells.
source: And third, we documented the dynamics of polarity sites in yeast cells, supporting coexistence as the dominant mechanism for multi-polar outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Increasing numbers of polarity sites with cell size is predicted by different classes of simple mathematical pattern-formation models.
source: Increasing numbers of polarity sites with cell size is predicted by different classes of simple mathematical pattern-formation models relevant to polarity establishment.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Classical Turing models exhibit a characteristic length scale such that local peaks form at spatial intervals corresponding to this length scale.
source: Classical (not mass-conserved) turing models exhibit a characteristic length scale, such that local peaks of an activator form spontaneously at spatial intervals corresponding to this length scale. Cells develop one or more peaks depending on how large the cell is compared to the characteristic length scale (Cornwall Scoones et al., 2020; Meinhardt, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: MCAS models can develop variable numbers of initial activator peaks that compete with each other as substrate is depleted.
source: Mass-conserved activator-substrate (MCAS) models can develop variable numbers of initial activator peaks, but as substrate is depleted from the cytoplasm the peaks compete with each other. Eventually, competition leads to a single-peak steady state, but the timescale of competition slows dramatically as the total abundance of activator/substrate in the system is increased (Brauns et al., 2020a; Chiou et al., 2018; Ishihara et al., 2007; Otsuji et al., 2010), yielding coexistence on biologically relevant timescales.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: More complex MCAS models can switch from competition to equalization as parameters change.
source: More complex MCAS models can switch from a regime exhibiting competition (where a larger peak grows faster than a smaller peak) to a regime exhibiting equalization (where a smaller peak grows faster than a larger peak) as parameters change (Howell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: The number of initial polarity sites may reflect the specifics of the experimental system rather than a feature of classical Turing systems.
source: Thus, the number of initial polarity sites may reflect the specifics of our experimental system rather than a feature of classical Turing systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Competition emerges as a consequence of mass conservation in MCAS models.
source: Competition emerges as a consequence of mass conservation, and suggests that MCAS models provide the explanation that best fits the behavior of the yeast system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the experimental observations.

claim: Aborted competition is at odds with MCAS model predictions where competition accelerates and always goes to completion.
source: This behavior is at odds with the predictions of MCAS models, in which competition accelerates as the amount of activator in the peaks becomes more uneven and always goes to completion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a discrepancy between experimental observations and model predictions.

claim: Some aspect of the polarity circuit may change at around the time of bud emergence, reducing the efficacy of competition.
source: This discrepancy may indicate that some aspect of the polarity circuit changes at around the time of bud emergence, reducing the efficacy of competition. Cell cycle control by the cyclin/CDK system provides one plausible candidate regulator that could prompt such a change in polarity circuit behavior (Knaus et al., 2007; Moran et al., 2019; Sopko et al., 2007; Witte et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation supported by citations.

claim: All multibudded cells observed had buds emanating from different cell lobes.
source: While competition could occur between peaks in the same or different lobes of cytokinesis-defective cells, all of the multibudded cells we observed had buds emanating from different cell lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on experimental observations.

claim: Competition is more effective within a lobe than between lobes in cytokinesis-defective cells.
source: This observation suggests that competition is more effective within a lobe than between lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The geometrical narrowing at the neck of multi-lobed cells slightly retards diffusional communication between lobes.
source: A possible basis for this effect is that the geometrical narrowing at the neck of multi-lobed cells slightly retards diffusional communication between lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the geometry of the cells.

claim: Saturation is the dominant factor determining the timescale of competition in minimalistic MCAS models.
source: Analyses of minimalistic two-component MCAS models demonstrated that competition between activator peaks was inevitable, and that the timescale of competition was determined by a single dominant factor, which we refer to as saturation (Brauns et al., 2020a; Chiou et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2019; Otsuji et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Findings from minimalistic MCAS models hold in a more complex model of the yeast polarity circuit.
source: We show that these findings from minimalistic one-activator, one-substrate models hold in a more complex and realistic model of the yeast polarity circuit, with two activators, two substrates, and two intermediate species, with some additional complexity discussed below.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the modeling results.

claim: In multi-component MCAS models, substrate depletion and activator concentration profiles can vary for different protein species.
source: In the multi-component model, substrate depletion and the activator concentration profile can vary for different protein species.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results.

claim: For the limiting species in multi-component MCAS models, addition of more protein leads to depletion of cytoplasmic substrate.
source: For the limiting species, addition of more protein will generally lead to depletion of the cytoplasmic substrate, similar to saturation in the minimalistic models.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results.

claim: Non-limiting species in multi-component MCAS models can display increasing cytoplasmic substrate concentration as more protein is added.
source: However, other (non-limiting) species can display increasing cytoplasmic substrate concentration as more protein is added.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results.

claim: Addition of one species can lead to a switch in the identity of the limiting species in multi-component MCAS models.
source: Moreover, addition of one species can lead to a switch in the identity of the limiting species.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results.

claim: Negative feedback is neither necessary nor sufficient to produce equalization in MCAS models.
source: However, we found that negative feedback was neither necessary nor sufficient to produce equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results.

claim: The key features enabling equalization are: the new species is produced from an activator, produces substrate, and is more mobile than the activator.
source: The key features of an additional species that enable equalization are as follows. First, the new species is produced from (or by) an activator. Second, the new species produces substrate. Third, the new species must be more mobile than the activator.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling analysis.

claim: A larger activator peak produces more of the new species than a smaller peak, yielding a flux that can produce equalization.
source: A larger activator peak produces more of the new species than a smaller peak, yielding a flux of mobile species from the larger peak to the smaller peak that can produce equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for equalization.

claim: Rapid mobility of the indirect substrate is essential for equalization.
source: When the indirect substrate diffused slowly (comparable to the activator), the system exclusively displayed competition or coexistence, indicating that rapid mobility of the indirect substrate is essential for equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: When the indirect substrate diffuses much faster than the substrate, the system exhibits classical Turing behavior.
source: At the other extreme, when the indirect substrate diffused much faster than the substrate, the system exhibited classical (not mass conserved) Turing behavior, generating peaks separated by a characteristic wavelength.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the modeling results.

claim: In the limit of infinite diffusion of the indirect substrate, the mass-conserved system resembles models that do not assume mass conservation.
source: We note that in the limit of infinite diffusion of the indirect substrate, this mass-conserved system would resemble some models that do not assume mass conservation (Brauns et al., 2020a; Jacobs et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The yeast polarity circuit has several species that could provide indirect pathways from activator to substrate.
source: Moreover, the yeast polarity circuit has several other species that could similarly provide indirect pathways from activator to substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on knowledge of the yeast polarity circuit.

claim: The physiological parameter space in which the yeast polarity circuit operates is not prone to equalization.
source: However, we detect very few cases of possible equalization in the cells we analyzed, suggesting that the physiological parameter space in which this circuit operates is not prone to equalization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental observations.

claim: MCAS circuits produce desirable outcomes for morphogenetic biological systems in a robust manner.
source: MCAS circuits are now recognized to produce desirable outcomes for morphogenetic biological systems, including polarization, in a robust manner (Goryachev and Leda, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Cell size can effectively control the number of polarity sites that form in MCAS circuits.
source: One property that can effectively control the number of polarity sites that form is cell size (Cornwall Scoones et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: There is a minimum cell size below which MCAS circuits are unable to polarize.
source: For example, there is a minimum size below which MCAS circuits are unable to polarize at all, and recent work indicates that the decrease in cell size that occurs during worm embryogenesis causes a switch from asymmetric cell division of polarized large cells to symmetric division of unpolarized small cells (Hubatsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe naturally switch from uni-polar to bi-polar growth during each cell cycle.
source: Schizosaccharomyces pombe naturally switch from uni-polar to bi-polar growth during each cell cycle (Grallert et al., 2013; Martin and Chang, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Ashbya gossypii form branching hyphae that exhibit increasing number of polarity sites as each cell grows.
source: Ashbya gossypii, which evolved relatively recently from a common ancestor with S. cerevisiae, form branching hyphae that exhibit increasing number of polarity sites as each cell grows (Knechtle et al., 2003; Schmitz and Philippsen, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The correlation between cell size and number of polarity sites suggests that cell size and higher abundance of polarity factors may trigger the increase in number of polarity sites.
source: The correlation between cell size and number of polarity sites in these systems suggests that, as proposed for MCAS models, cell size and the associated higher abundance of polarity factors may trigger the increase in number of polarity sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference based on observations in different systems.

claim: Yeast cells of Aureobasidium sp. generate variable numbers of buds simultaneously.
source: Most remarkably, yeast cells of Aureobasidium sp. generate variable numbers of buds simultaneously (Mitchison-Field et al., 2019), a capacity shared with the much more distantly related zygomycete Mucor circinelloides (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Phenotypic diversity in polarity may be enabled by a polarity circuit that allows a switch between competition, coexistence, and equalization behaviors.
source: This phenotypic diversity may be enabled by a polarity circuit that allows a switch between competition, coexistence, and equalization behaviors in response to appropriate tuning of parameter values.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the findings.
